1.pericope_label: If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above — set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth

schools.summary: Give the chapter its analysis first, numbering the duties enjoined in order: the setting of the affections on things above, the mortifying of corrupt passions, the speaking of truth, kindness and gentleness and the spirit of peace, the edifying of one another by psalms, and then the duties of wives and husbands and children and fathers and servants. Render the opening clause rather as ye rose, and mark in it the beginning of the spiritual life, referred evidently to baptism, a resurrection with Christ and in Christ. Draw from the phrase an argument about practice: implying as it does a sudden passing from death unto life, it accords more exactly with the idea of adult baptism, accepted in conscious faith and leading at once to a new life, whereas the later word regeneration, which speaks of the soul as passing at once into a new condition but as having only the undeveloped germ of the new life, corresponds more closely with the idea of the infant baptism which gradually superseded the other. Note that the name of Christ, four times repeated, has the article prefixed in every case, evidently used emphatically of our Lord as Mediator, our Prophet and Priest and King. Call the condition one of the first class, assumed as true, and observe that what is given here in place of merely ascetic rules is an ideal and a goal, the upward things, the treasure in heaven, Christ being up there and at God’s right hand. Then name the earthly things plainly — wealth, honour, pleasure, houses and lands, scenes of fashion and gaiety, and low and debasing enjoyments — while glossing the verb as keep on thinking about, and remarking that it does matter what we think and that we are responsible for our thoughts. And refuse to make the command otherworldly: it is not meant that we should never think the things upon the earth, but that these should not be our aim, our goal, our master, since the Christian has to keep his feet upon the earth but his head in the heavens, and must be heavenly-minded here on earth and so help to make earth like heaven.

Take the rising for granted rather than calling it in question, and distinguish the senses in which it happened: representatively, when Christ rose as their head and they as members in union with him; emblematically in baptism, when having gone down into the water they emerged from it; and spiritually in conversion, when they were raised from a death of sin to a life of grace by Christ as the resurrection and the life. Argue from it how much it becomes them to regard a new and spiritual life, to seek after superior and heavenly things, and to treat carnal and earthly ones with neglect. Explain the affection as a minding and thinking, a favouring and approving, an affectionate desire, since where the treasure is the heart should be, and the saints’ best things being above, their minds and affections should be there also, their citizenship being in heaven where in a short time they must have their everlasting residence. Then set the whole exhortation against the false teachers: to the fruitless exercises which they urged as though perfection consisted in them, oppose the true exercises in which it becomes Christians to employ themselves, since when we see what God would have us do we afterwards easily despise the inventions of men, and when we perceive that what God recommends is more lofty than what men inculcate our alacrity for following God increases. This doctrine therefore makes the ceremonies be the more lightly esteemed, and the vanity of human traditions vanish into smoke; and it anticipates the objection the false teachers might raise, whether you would rather have men idle than addicted to exercises of some sort. And narrow the earthly things accordingly: not depraved appetites, nor riches or fields or houses or any other things of the present life which we must use as though we did not use them, but still the ceremonies, which resemble entanglements constraining us to creep upon the ground — Christ calling us upwards to himself while these draw us downwards. Do not contend against those of a different mind, but hold that the argument goes on step by step.

Having described our privileges by Christ in the former part of the epistle, and our discharge from the yoke of the ceremonial law, press upon us our duty as inferred from it: though we are made free from the obligation of the ceremonial law, it does not therefore follow that we may live as we list, but we must walk the more closely with God in all the instances of evangelical obedience. Begin by exhorting them to set their hearts on heaven and take them off from this world, since it is our privilege that we have risen with Christ, that is, have benefit by his resurrection, and by virtue of our union and communion with him are justified and sanctified and shall be glorified. Infer from this that we must seek the things above: we must mind the concerns of another world more than the concerns of this, make heaven our scope and aim, seek the favour of God above, keep up our communion with the upper world by faith and hope and holy love, and make it our constant care and business to secure our title to and qualifications for the heavenly bliss. And give the reason simply, because Christ sits at the right hand of God.

Set out the argument of the chapter before beginning, from the exhortation to heavenly-mindedness after the example of Christ, through the mortifying of the members, the change from the former state, the directions as to truth and compassion and meekness and forgiveness, the call to unity and holiness and to having the doctrine of Christ dwelling richly in them, and so to the relative duties of wives, husbands, children, fathers and servants, and the closing warning that he who does wrong shall be treated accordingly, since God is no respecter of persons. Refer the opening clause back to the burial and rising in baptism spoken of in the previous chapter. Then turn the command into a rule of exchange: love heavenly things, study them, let your hearts be entirely engrossed by them; now that you are converted to God, act in reference to heavenly things as you did formerly in reference to those of earth, and the reverse — which is a very good general rule, that you be as much in earnest for heavenly and eternal things as you formerly were for those that are earthly and perishing. And compress the ground of the whole into a clause, that Christ, being risen, immediately went to heaven.

Use the verse not as an exhortation but as a testimony, collecting it with the other proofs of the Son’s sitting at the right hand of the Father: that in the Gospel where he says they shall see the Son of Man sitting on the right hand of power; that in the apostle Peter, who writes of the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who is on the right hand of God, having gone into heaven; that in the letter to the Romans, that it is Christ who died, yea rather who is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God; that in the charge to the Ephesians, according to the working of his mighty power which he wrought in Christ when he raised him from the dead and set him at his own right hand; this one to the Colossians, if ye then be risen with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; and that in the letter to the Hebrews, when he had made purification.

Expound a passage of another epistle, where the several motives of those who were preaching the gospel are mentioned — some waxing confident by his bonds and more fearless in speaking the word, others preaching Christ even out of envy and strife, others out of good will, many out of love, certain out of contention, and some in rivalry to himself. There was a favourable opportunity here of taxing what they preached with a diversity of doctrine, as if that were what caused so great a variance in their tempers; but while exposing the tempers as the sole cause of the diversity, he avoids inculpating the regular mysteries of the faith and affirms that there is notwithstanding but one Christ and his one God, whatever the motives of those who preached him. Therefore he says it matters not whether it be in pretence or in truth that Christ is preached, because one Christ alone was announced; for it was to the faithfulness of their preaching that he applied the word truth, not to the rightness of the rule itself, since there was but one rule while the conduct of the preachers varied.

debates: Whether the rising spoken of is assumed or argued for.
In what senses believers may be said to have risen with Christ.
What the things on the earth are that must not be minded.
Whether the command forbids all thought of earthly things.
What the exhortation has to do with the argument of the previous chapter.
outliers: Ellicott argues from the vocabulary of this verse that adult baptism was the original practice and infant baptism superseded it.
Calvin alone identifies the earthly things with the ceremonies rather than with wealth or pleasure.
Barnes names wealth, honour, houses and lands where Calvin expressly excludes them.
Robertson denies that the command forbids thinking of earthly things at all.
Gill distinguishes three distinct senses of having risen with Christ.
Two of the blocks printed at the first verse expound other epistles or the chapter as a whole rather than this verse.

3.pericope_label: For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God — when Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory

schools.summary: Take the death by exclusion, ruling out three senses before allowing a fourth: it is not natural or corporeal, for they were living in the world; not moral, for though they had been dead in sins they were quickened by the grace of God; not legal, for all their trespasses were forgiven them. What remains is that they were dead to the law, moral and ceremonial and judicial, by the body of Christ; dead to sin as to its damning power, through his bearing it in his own body on the tree; and dead to the world by his cross — so that as dead men have nothing to do with the world, believers should have no regard to the rudiments of the world, the ceremonies of the law and the ordinances of men, nor to the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes and the pride of life. Reverse the direction of the argument elsewhere, reasoning from the consequent to the antecedent, since no one can rise again with Christ who has not first died with him, so that we must be dead to the world in order to live to Christ, and both must be seen in us. Then ask what the hiddenness is for, and answer that our life is said to be hidden so that we may not murmur or complain if our life, being buried under the ignominy of the cross and under various distresses, differs nothing from death, but may patiently wait for the day of revelation; and lest the waiting be painful, observe two securities — that God is faithful and will not deny what has been committed to him, nor deceive in the guardianship he has undertaken, and that the fellowship of Christ brings a greater security still. Call the appearing a choice consolation, since the coming of Christ will be the manifestation of our life, and add how unreasonable is the disposition of the man who should refuse to bear up until that day, for if our life is shut up in Christ it must remain so until he appears. Note the variant by which some copies and one ancient version read your life for our life; and say that Christ is the author of spiritual life, the fountain from which it springs, the object on which the saints live and their very life itself, so that it is not so much they that live as Christ that lives in them.

Render the first clause ye died, mark it a definite event, and take it in its whole sense, both of death to sin and of death to the visible world; draw the comparison out, that as Christ became literally dead in the tomb, so in virtue of our connexion with him we have become dead to sin and to worldly influences and pleasures and ambition, or rather are to be to them as if we were dead, and they had no more influence over us than the things of earth had over him in the grave. Make the hidden life a strongbox: the perfect tense has it remaining concealed, locked together with Christ and in God, and no hellish burglar can break that combination. Make it also a treasure laid up in a place of security, an invaluable jewel deposited with the Redeemer in the presence of God, so that nothing can reach it or take it away — observing that it is not left with us or entrusted to our keeping, for then it might be lost, or wrested from us, or we might be defrauded of it. Then read the four verses as one structure: the first marks the beginning of the spiritual life, referred to baptism, the middle describes its continuance, and the last its close in glorification, manifesting what is now hidden and perfecting what exists only in germ. Note the movement from the lower expression to the higher, since it is one thing to say that our life is hid with Christ and another that Christ is our life, the two together summarising that Christ liveth in me as the source of life and that to me to live is Christ. Conclude that the whole passage forms a complete and magnificent picture of the spiritual life in Christ, the means of its beginning, the signs of its presence and the hope of its close. And on the appearing, make the temporal clause indefinite, whenever Christ is manifested, a reference to the second coming as looked for and longed for but wholly uncertain as to time, adding that not to respond to so high an appeal is to be like the man with the muck-rake.

Take the death as a death to all hopes of happiness from the present world, so that by their profession they should feel no more appetite for the things of this life than a man whose soul has departed into the invisible state. Turn the hidden life back on the heart: Christ is your treasure, and where your treasure is there is your heart; Christ lives in the bosom of the Father, and as your heart is in him you also sit in heavenly places with Christ Jesus, for Christ is the life of your souls, and as he is hidden in the bosom of the Father, so are you who live through him and in him. Say elsewhere that the real and spiritual life is hidden from the world and laid up in God with him who has merited and promised and prepared it for us, and who gives us the earnest and foretaste of it in our hearts. Refer the appearing to the day when Christ comes to judge the world, when you shall appear with him in his glory and in an eternal state of blessedness. And catch the effect of the syntax: the abruptness of the sentence surrounds us with sudden light — our life, the fountain of holiness and glory, shall appear in the clouds of heaven.

debates: In what sense the readers are said to be dead.
What the hiddenness of the life is for.
Whether the life is kept by us or for us.
How the four verses hang together.
What the appearing refers to.
outliers: Gill rules out three senses of the death before allowing the one he holds.
Robertson makes the hidden life a locked combination no hellish burglar can break.
Barnes argues that the life is not entrusted to our keeping precisely because we could lose it.
Calvin makes the hiddenness a remedy against complaint under affliction.
Ellicott reads the four verses as a complete picture of the spiritual life from beginning to close.
Wesley notices that the abruptness of the syntax is itself part of the effect.

5.pericope_label: Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth — for which things’ sake the wrath of God cometh on the children of disobedience

schools.summary: Call the expression doubly unique: it is the only passage where mortification, the killing of anything in us, is enjoined, and it is notable for not explicitly distinguishing between the members themselves and the evil of which they are made the instruments. Note that the sense is clear enough and corresponds to the crucifying of the flesh elsewhere, the idea of evil being hinted in the phrase about being on the earth, that is, busied with earth and binding us down to the earthly life; suggest that the particular word members was perhaps prompted by the command to cut off the right hand and pluck out the right eye if they cause us to offend. But add that as a rule Scripture marks more clearly the distinction between the members and the law of sin in the members, and that we are usually bidden not to kill our members but to turn them from instruments of unrighteousness to instruments of righteousness unto God — so that this passage contains only half the truth. Define the verb as to put to death, to treat as dead, and remark that the English word is drifting towards the sense of putrefying; observe that the metaphor of death pictured in baptism is here boldly applied to the actual life of the Christian, who is not to go to the other extreme of license on the plea that the soul is not affected by the deeds of the body, since the body is the temple of the Holy Spirit. List the vices named and note that covetousness is absent from the longer catalogue of the works of the flesh elsewhere though present in another epistle. Insist that these sins of the flesh are no matter of indifference, far otherwise, and note that many old manuscripts lack the clause about the sons of disobedience, which is genuine in the parallel epistle. Then read the former state as an element: heathenism was that in which they were living, with contagion of evil on every side, but do not be content without noting their own active participation, since they walked in them; and mark the sharp distinction of the tenses, a constative aorist for the walking and an imperfect for the customary living.

Deny that the members meant are those of the natural body, and make them the members of the body of sin, indwelling sin being as a body that consists of various members which rise out of it and are used by it. Deny too that what is enjoined is a mortification of the body of sin itself, or of the being and principle of it in the soul, where it lives and dwells and will as long as the saints are in this tabernacle; what is meant is the deeds of the body as to the life and conversation, that is a denial of them, an abstinence from them and a non-performance of them. Distinguish elsewhere a twofold mortification, the former relating to the things around us, which has been treated hitherto, and the other inward, of the understanding and will and of the whole of our corrupt nature; grant that the vices are called members not with strict accuracy but at the same time elegantly, since our nature is conceived as a mass made up of different vices which in a manner stick close to us; and note that they are called earthly in allusion to the earlier phrase but in a different sense, since we are earthly so long as the vices of our flesh are vigorous in us. On the wrath, refuse to fix the tense: the present is often taken in Scripture for the future after the Hebrew idiom, so leave the rendering undecided to suit either meaning — the ordinary judgments of God, which are seen daily, or the vengeance once denounced upon the wicked, which impends but will not be manifested until the last day — while inclining to the former. And observe what the sentence does not do: it says expressly that the wrath will come upon the unbelieving, instead of threatening the readers with anything of the kind, for God would rather that we should see his wrath upon the reprobate than feel it in ourselves. Then separate living from walking as power differs from action, living holding the first place and walking coming after, and correct the rendering which referred the phrase to men rather than to the vices — it being an unseemly thing that they should addict themselves any more to vices to which they had died. And make sin a road in which sinners walk a way of their own choosing, dark and crooked, walking there denoting a continued series of sinning, a persisting and a progress from evil to evil.

Render the verb put them to death, the word being used metaphorically for depriving a thing of its power and destroying its strength: use no member of your body to sin against God, keep all under dominion, and never permit the beast to run away with the man. Add the rule about appetite: to gratify any sensual appetite is to give it the very food and nourishment by which it lives and thrives and is active, and however the body may suffer by excessive indulgence, the appetite increases with the indulgence — therefore deny yourselves and let reason rule, and the animal will not get the ascendency over the rational man. Gloss the vices in turn, the third as unnatural and degrading passion, the fourth as strong desire joined with the word evil to fix the sense. Say the covetous man makes his money his god, since it is the prerogative of God to confer happiness. Elsewhere make the killing a slaying with a continued stroke, place the members upon the earth where they find their nourishment, and take the vices as uncleanness in act or word or thought, every passion which does not flow from and lead to the love of God, and the desire of the flesh and of the eye and the pride of life. Derive covetousness as the desire of having more, or of anything independent of God, and call it idolatry properly and directly, since it is giving the heart to a creature. Say of the wrath only that the heathen regarded these things lightly. And distinguish in nine words that living denotes the inward principle and walking the outward acts.

Make the mortification of sin the great hindrance removed: since it is our duty to set our affections on heavenly things, it is our duty to mortify the members that are upon the earth and naturally incline us to the things of the world. Put the command as extermination — subdue the vicious habits of mind that prevailed in your former state; kill them, suppress them, as you do weeds or vermin which spread and destroy all about them, or as you kill an enemy who fights against you and wounds you. Allow the members to be either the members of the body, which are the earthly part of us and were curiously wrought in the lower parts of the earth, or the corrupt affections of the mind which lead us to earthly things, the members of the body of death. And specify what is named: the lusts of the flesh, for which they were before so remarkable, the various workings of the carnal appetites and fleshly impurities which they indulged in their former state.

Preach the verse as an apology to a congregation. I know that many are offended by the foregoing discourse, but what can I do? You heard what the Master enjoined; am I to blame? See the creditors, how when debtors are obstinate they wear collars. Heard you what was proclaimed today, to mortify your members which are upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry? What is worse than such a covetousness? This is worse than any desire, and more grievous than the madness and silly weakness about silver of which I was speaking. See in what the evil ends. Do not take what I said amiss, for not by my own good will, nor without reason, would I have enemies; I was wishful you should attain to such virtue as that I might hear of you the things I ought. So that I said it not for authority’s sake, nor out of imperiousness, but out of pain and of sorrow. Forgive me, forgive: I have no wish to violate decency by discoursing upon such subjects, but I am compelled to it.

debates: Whether the members to be killed are bodily or the vices themselves.
Whether sin itself or only its deeds can be put to death.
How far the command may be pressed as a rule.
Whether the wrath spoken of is present or future.
What distinguishes living in sins from walking in them.
outliers: Ellicott says outright that this passage contains only half the truth and that Scripture usually teaches the other half.
Gill denies that the principle of indwelling sin can be destroyed in this life, and confines the command to its deeds.
Chrysostom’s note is an apology to hearers offended by his previous sermon rather than a comment on the verse.
Clarke observes that appetite grows by the indulgence that damages the body.
Calvin refuses to settle the tense of the wrath and leaves the rendering undecided.
Calvin and Wesley independently distinguish living as the inward principle from walking as the outward act.

8.pericope_label: Put off all these: anger, wrath, malice — lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds, and have put on the new man — where there is neither Greek nor Jew

schools.summary: Notice that one figure governs the whole passage: the metaphor is clothing, and it runs through four verbs in as many verses — laying aside like old clothes, stripping clean off, putting on, and putting on again — the whole bunch of vices being so many filthy rags. Take the word usually rendered blasphemy to mean all injurious and calumnious speaking, whether against God or man; and on the next word either make it lewd, indecent and immodest discourse, an old word for low and obscene speech occurring here alone in the New Testament, or else hold that the context points to grossness of insult and abuse rather than to filthiness. Render the prohibition of lying either as stop lying or as do not have the habit of lying; call the vice a universal fruit of sin and doubt whether any single form of sin reigns so universally where the gospel has not prevailed. Notice what is missing, that the parallel epistle adds a clause with nothing here to answer it, namely that we are members one of another, the reason given here being instead that the old man has been put off. Distinguish the two Greek words for new, the one here meaning young as against the ancient man and the one in the parallel epistle meaning fresh as against the worn out, so that the sense is a continual refreshment of the young man in Christ; add that the verb for renewing appears to have been coined on the analogy of another, and that the writer mixes his metaphors as he often does, the old life being at once a garment stripped off and a man already crucified. Argue doctrine from the pairing with the parallel passage, that since knowledge is added there to righteousness and true holiness, man before he fell was endowed with all three, the knowledge meant being not of everything but of God, and especially that knowledge which is the fear of the Lord. Then read the list of abolished distinctions by what it adds and omits: the insertion of barbarian and Scythian, absent from the parallel elsewhere, is clearly intended to rebuke that pride of intellect, contemptuous of the unlearned, which lay at the root of the local error, the barbarian being simply the foreigner and the Scythian the savage in whom contempt reached its climax; while the omission of male and female is explained by the different dangers of the two societies, since in one the dignity of women needed to be asserted and in the other the new freedom of the gospel was apt to be abused to license. Locate the Scythians north and north-east of the Black and Caspian Seas; and call the whole verse an ideal still a long way ahead of modern Christians, as the late war proved.

Take the putting off as a consequence of conversion: now that they are delivered out of their former state and profess not to walk in sin, it becomes them to separate and remove and put at a distance every vice, to lay them aside as dead weights and put them off as filthy garments, never to be put on and cleaved to again. Note that the second word for anger denotes a more impetuous passionateness than the first, and that the vices here enumerated differ from those named before. Widen the prohibition of lying beyond calumny to every sort of cunning and all base artifices of deception, taking it as contrasted in a general way with sincerity, so that it might as well be rendered more briefly still; and add that it is the more unnatural among those who are members one of another and of the same body. Then define the two men: the old denotes whatever we bring from our mother’s womb and whatever we are by nature, and is put off by all who are renewed by Christ; the new is that which is renewed by the Spirit of Christ to the obedience of righteousness, or nature restored to its true integrity by the same Spirit. Deny that a simple and bare knowledge is meant by the renewing, and make it the illumination of the Holy Spirit, lively and effectual, not merely enlightening the mind by kindling it with the light of truth but transforming the whole man; note that the image resides in the whole of the soul, since it is not the reason merely that is rectified but also the will, and learn from this both the end of our regeneration, that we may be made like God and his glory shine forth in us, and what the image of God is. And say that the list of distinctions was added intentionally to draw the readers away from ceremonies once more, since Christian perfection does not stand in need of outward observances but is altogether at variance with them.

Set the passions beside the appetites: as we are to mortify inordinate appetites, so we are to mortify inordinate passions, for these are contrary to the design of the gospel as well as the grosser impurities, and though they are more spiritual wickedness they have not less malignity in them. Observe that the gospel introduces a change of the higher as well as the lower powers of the soul, and supports the dominion of right reason and conscience over appetite and passion. Grade the vices named: anger and wrath are bad, but malice is worse, because it is more rooted and deliberate, being anger heightened and settled. And observe that as the corrupt principles in the heart must be cut off, so must their product in the tongue — the word rendered blasphemy seeming to mean not so much speaking ill of God as speaking ill of men, giving them ill language or raising ill reports of them and injuring their good name by any evil arts.

Say that being now converted, sin had no more dominion over them, so that they had not only laid aside the grosser evils named before but these also, retaining no bosom or easily besetting sin. Take the word rendered blasphemy to mean injurious and calumnious speaking. Bring the prohibition of lying down to the market: do not deceive each other but speak the truth in all your dealings, and do not undervalue your neighbour’s goods when your conscience tells you otherwise, for the buyer says it is naught, it is naught, and afterwards boasts — underrating his neighbour’s property till he gets him to part with it for less than its worth, and then boasting what a good bargain he has made. Turn the renewal on the heathen: ignorance was the grand characteristic of the heathen state and knowledge of the Christian, since the utmost heathenism could pretend to was a certain knowledge of nature, whereas Christianity teaches a man the true knowledge both of himself and of God — and it is impossible to know oneself but in the light of God, so that the famous injunction to know thyself was practicable only under the Christian religion. On the abolished distinctions, say that no inquiry is made what nation the persons belonged to, nor what form of religion they had, nor whether they were of the more or less tractable of the nations, since under the teaching of the Spirit the most dull are perfectly capable of comprehending this divine science; nor does a man’s state help him to or exclude him from the benefit, the slave having as good a title to salvation by grace as the freeman. And express surprise that the warning was needed: was there need to warn even these saints of God against so gross and palpable a sin, and what is man until perfect love casts out both fear and sin?

Give the putting off its most vivid figure. If any here is a slave of sin, let him prepare himself through faith for the new birth into freedom and adoption, and having put off the miserable bondage of his sins and taken on him the most blessed bondage of the Lord, so may he be counted worthy to inherit the kingdom of heaven. Put off, by confession, the old man which waxeth corrupt after the lusts of deceit, that ye may put on the new man which is renewed according to knowledge of him that created him; come for the mystical seal, that ye may be easily recognised by the Master and numbered among the holy flock, since they to whom the rough garment of their sins still clings are found on the left hand. And press the same by the serpent: be not henceforth a viper, but as thou hast formerly been a viper’s brood, put off the slough of thy former sinful life — for every serpent creeps into a hole and casts its old slough, and having rubbed off the old skin grows young again in body.

debates: What single figure governs the run of commands.
Whether the words condemned are obscene speech or abusive speech.
On what ground lying is forbidden here rather than elsewhere.
What the renewal in knowledge implies about man before the fall.
Why barbarian and Scythian are added to the list of abolished distinctions.
outliers: Robertson traces one clothing metaphor through four verbs in four verses.
Ellicott reads the disputed word as insult and abuse; Barnes and Robertson read it as obscenity.
Ellicott and Barnes independently note that the parallel epistle gives a different reason for the same command.
Barnes infers from the pairing of two passages that unfallen man possessed knowledge as well as righteousness.
Ellicott explains both the insertion of barbarian and Scythian and the omission of male and female by the local situation.
Robertson dates his own comment by measuring the verse against the late war.
Cyril of Jerusalem makes the putting off a serpent shedding its slough and growing young again.

12.pericope_label: Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies — forbearing one another, and forgiving one another — and above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness

schools.summary: Read the imperative as the application of the new man under the figure of the new garment, and list the items of the new clothing against what was put off: a heart of compassion, the nobler seat of emotion, kindness, humility in the good sense, meekness, long-suffering, each with its parallels elsewhere in the letters. Note that in the Gospels a distinction exists between called and chosen but that no such distinction appears in this writer. Take the title elect of God of the whole Church, as election to privilege, not opposed to called but coincident with it, representing the secret act of God’s gracious will which is openly manifested in calling; and find in the two epithets holy and beloved the two signs of that election, consecration to God in thought and life and acceptance in his love, both belonging to them as conformed to the image of Christ, who is himself the Holy One of God and the Beloved. Observe that the two epithets are meant to prepare for the two-fold exhortation that follows, since they are beloved and should therefore love one another, and holy and should therefore give thanks and live to his glory. On forgiveness, resolve the duty into its parts: harbour no malice, be ready to do the man good as if he had given no occasion of complaint, be willing to declare the forgiveness when it is asked, and ever afterwards treat him as kindly as if he had not injured us, as God treats us when he forgives; and find the same properties in the pattern, that Christ forgave freely without hesitation or delay, entirely, pardoning all offences, and for ever, remembering the sins no more. Note that the word for the ground of complaint occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, that the first participle governs the ablative and means holding yourselves back from one another, and that the second takes the reflexive pronoun where the first took the reciprocal. On the disputed name, say the manuscript authority favours Lord rather than Christ, but that since Lord is specially applied to Christ in these letters there is no real difference. Then take the bond of perfectness as the girdle holding the various garments together, the genitive being one of apposition; and add that the remarkable phrase was apparently suggested by the claim to perfection set up by the local teachers, who sought perfection in a knowledge peculiar to the few where the apostle sought it in the love possible to all — knowledge puffs up, charity builds up. Say plainly that love binds all the other graces fast together and renders the whole system complete, so that without it there would be a painful want of harmony though every other grace were present, and that neither faith nor zeal nor prophecy nor the power of speaking with the tongue of angels would answer the purpose instead.

Take the graces enumerated as the effects and evidences of renovation, so that it appears men are renewed by Christ only when they are merciful and gentle; and keep the metaphor of clothing in the verb. Distinguish the terms as they come: first an earnest affection with yearnings of the heart, then the kindness by which we make ourselves amiable, then the humility without which no one will be kind and gentle, since haughtiness must be laid aside before a man will claim nothing for himself; and note that the term which follows has a wider acceptation than gentleness, for gentleness is chiefly in look and speech while this is also in the inward disposition. Add that since we frequently come in contact with wicked and ungrateful men there is need of patience to cherish mildness in us, and that even just occasions of quarrel, according to the views of men, ought not to be followed out. Read the whole as a condition: God has chosen you to himself, has sanctified you and received you into his love on this condition, that ye be merciful, and to no purpose does the man who lacks these excellences boast that he is holy and beloved of God or reckon himself among the number of believers. On the last verse, prefer the ordinary sense of the preposition, over all these things, and call love the bond of perfectness because the whole troop of the virtues is comprehended under it, this being the rule of our whole life and of all our actions, so that everything not regulated by it is faulty whatever attractiveness it may otherwise possess. Then refuse the inference drawn from the verse in support of justification by works — that love is the bond of perfectness, that perfection is righteousness, and that therefore we are justified by love. The answer is twofold. The apostle is not reasoning here as to the manner in which men are made perfect in the sight of God, but as to the manner in which they may live perfectly among themselves; and even granting that love is righteousness, the inference is childish, for where will perfect love be found? We say men are justified by faith alone not because the observance of the law is not righteousness, but because, being all of us transgressors of the law, we can find no righteousness there. Also say of the putting on of the graces that the clothing is a becoming garment, and that they are not a robe of righteousness or garments of salvation, since those are had already, but conversation garments, adorning to the wearer, to the doctrine of Christ and to the profession of it, without which a man walks naked and exposed to shame — a coat of many colours like Joseph’s.

Draw the moral shape of the passage. We must not only put off anger and wrath but put on compassion and kindness, not only cease to do evil but learn to do well, not only do hurt to none but do what good we can to all. Those who are holy are the elect of God, and those who are the elect of God and holy are beloved of God and ought to be so of all men; and it becomes those who are holy towards God to be lowly and loving towards all men. Take the particulars one by one: compassion towards the miserable, since those who owe so much to mercy ought to be merciful to all proper objects of it; kindness towards our friends, the design of the gospel being not only to soften the minds of men but to sweeten them; humbleness of mind, in submission to those above us and condescension to those below, and there must not only be a humble demeanour but a humble mind; meekness towards those who have provoked us, bridling our own anger prudently and bearing the anger of others patiently; long-suffering towards those who continue to provoke, since many can bear a short provocation who are weary of bearing when it grows long; mutual forbearance, since we all of us have something which needs to be borne with; and a readiness to forgive injuries. Grant that while we are in this world, where there is so much corruption in our hearts and so much occasion of difference, quarrels will sometimes happen even among the elect of God who are holy and beloved, as Paul and Barnabas had a sharp contention which parted them asunder, and as Paul withstood Peter. Then on the last verse, let charity be the upper garment, the robe, the livery, the mark of our dignity and distinction, principal and chief as the whole sum of the second table; lay the foundation in faith and the top-stone in charity, which is the cement and centre of all happy society, Christian unity consisting of unanimity and mutual love.

Read the title first: the apostle’s principal design was to show that God had chosen the Gentiles and called them to the same privileges as the Jews, intending to make them as truly his people as the Jews ever were, and therefore he calls them the elect or chosen of God, and as the Jews who were formerly the elect were still beloved and called to be holy, so he calls these beloved and shows them they are called with the same holy calling; and say elsewhere, more briefly, that all who are thus renewed are elected of God, holy, and therefore the more beloved of him, holiness being the consequence of their election and God’s superior love the consequence of their holiness. On the bowels of mercies, insist on being merciful not in act merely but in spirit and affection, letting the heart dictate to the hand; and though to put on and to be clothed with are figurative expressions meaning to assume such and such characters and qualities, suspect a higher meaning here, since as their clothes are put over their body so their tenderest feeling should be always within the reach of the miserable — let your feelings be at hand, and feel and commiserate as soon as touched. Add the textual note, that instead of the plural mercies almost every manuscript of importance, with many of the fathers, reads the singular, and that this various reading makes scarcely any alteration in the sense. On forgiveness, avoid all occasions of irritating or provoking each other, and if you receive offence be instantly ready to forgive on the first acknowledgment of the fault, as Christ required no satisfaction and sought nothing in you but the broken contrite heart; but enter this caveat, that no man should for a moment harbour ill will in his heart to any, yet the offended party is not called actually to forgive till the offender with sorrow acknowledges his fault — he should be ready to forgive, and while he is so he can feel neither hatred nor malice, but as Christ does not forgive us till with penitent hearts we return acknowledging our offences, so those who have trespassed against a neighbour are not to expect any act of forgiveness from the person they have injured till they acknowledge the offence. On the last verse, make love the outer garment which envelopes all the clothing, so that even bowels of mercy are set in motion by love and derive from it all their feeling and promptitude to action; represent it as a girdle by which all the rest of the clothing is bound close about the body; say that love begets love, and that the more a man loves God and his neighbour the more he is enabled to do so, love while properly exercised being ever increasing and reproducing itself; and report that instead of perfection several reputable manuscripts, with the Old Latin, read unity, though the former is doubtless the genuine reading. Say also, most briefly, that the love of God contains the whole of Christian perfection and connects all the parts of it together.

debates: Whether elect of God is a title of privilege for the whole Church or a mark of the individual.
Whether the offended party must forgive at once or only when the offender acknowledges the fault.
Whether the bond of perfectness can be made to prove justification by love.
Whether the received plural mercies or the manuscript singular is to be read.
What perfection the phrase bond of perfectness answers to.
outliers: Ellicott reads the epithets holy and beloved as a deliberate preparation for the two exhortations that follow.
Clarke suspects the clothing language is more than figure: the feelings are to be worn where they can be reached.
Clarke sets a condition on forgiving that Barnes and Wesley do not: the offender must first acknowledge the fault.
Robertson notes the writer switches from the reciprocal to the reflexive pronoun between two parallel participles.
Ellicott reads the bond of perfectness as a direct answer to the perfection claimed by the local teachers.
Calvin refuses an inference drawn from the verse in favour of justification by works, on two separate grounds.
Clarke reports a rival reading, unity in place of perfectness, in several manuscripts and the Old Latin.

15.pericope_label: And let the peace of God rule in your hearts — let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs — and whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus

schools.summary: Settle the text first: the true reading is the peace of Christ, that which He gives and that which He is, the ordinary reading having no doubt been borrowed from Philippians; and simply print it so. Take the verse as a link between the exhortation to love of man before it and the exhortation to a loving and thankful service of God after it, the peace of Christ being the sense of unity in Him with our fellow-men and with God, to which we are called in one Body of which He is the Head. On the verb, note that it is commonly used of the Olympic and other games and means to be director or arbiter of the public games, to preside over them, preserve order and distribute the prizes; that it occurs here alone in the New Testament; and that the peace which God gives is to preside over the soul as the governor at the games presided, keeping everything in its place and saving the mind from tumult and disorder — for the soul is liable to the agitations of passion like an assembled multitude of men and needs something to preside over it and keep its faculties in order. Add that a spirit of thankfulness tends to promote harmony, an ungrateful people being commonly tumultuous, restless and dissatisfied, and that the imperative means keep on becoming thankful, a continuous obligation. On the word of Christ, observe that the precise phrase occurs only here, that elsewhere it is the word of the Lord or the word of God, that the genitive may be either the word delivered by Christ or the word about Christ, and that the verb means to make one’s home, to be at home, the preposition meaning in you and not among you. On the placing of in all wisdom, either say that the symmetry of the original, teaching in wisdom answering to singing in grace, connects the words with what follows rather than, as in our version, with what goes before; or say that it is not clear which way the phrase goes, that either punctuation makes good sense, and that the older Greek manuscripts had no punctuation at all. Distinguish the three kinds of song, the psalms of the Old Testament originally with musical accompaniment, hymns composed by Christians, and a general term for songs with or without instruments, noting that the same song can take all three names. Then make the large claim: the ascription to psalms and hymns of an office of teaching and admonition describes their real though indirect effect, for in the Church as in the world he who makes a people’s songs guides their minds as well as their hearts, and for good and for evil the hymns of the Christian Church have largely influenced her theology — it was said that if a man were allowed to make the ballads of a nation he cared not who made the laws, and it is truer still that he who makes the hymns of a church need care little who preaches or who makes the creed. Say too that without singing in the heart there is no real worship whatever the instrument or voice. Finally, take the closing rule as the first principle of all godly life, the main object of life being the glory of God, and as the principle of Christian life besides, since it does all in the name of Christ and looks up thankfully to God through His mediation; and observe that the household code which follows deals with the three great relations of life in close parallel with the other epistle, that the first relation is treated far more briefly here, and that the third is dwelt on with marked emphasis — we can hardly doubt that the presence of Onesimus, the runaway slave, suggested it.

Explain the peace as that which God has established among us, and note that the versions and the Alexandrian copy read the peace of Christ. Say it may be either the peace believers have with God, which passes all understanding and flows from a comfortable apprehension of interest in the blood and righteousness of Christ, or rather that peace which subsists among the saints themselves, of which God is the author. It rules when it is the governing principle, restraining the turbulent passions of anger, wrath and revenge, allaying undue heats, moderating the spirits and composing differences. Use the metaphor of the judge in the games, the umpire and moderator who determined whose the victory was and to whom the crown belonged, and say the apostle would have no other umpire among the saints than this peace; or take it from the wrestlers, since he who has vanquished all the rest carries off the palm, so peace is to be superior to all the carnal affections which hurry us into contentions, disagreements, quarrels and secret grudges, and is to be the bridle by which they are restrained. Add that the calling in one body means that we cannot be in agreement with God otherwise than by being united among ourselves as members of one body. On being thankful, prefer to render it be amiable, taking it to refer not so much to the remembrance of favours as to sweetness of manners, while acknowledging that if gratitude possesses our minds we shall not fail to cherish mutual affection. On the indwelling word, say the doctrine of the gospel is to be familiarly known, and infer what spirit actuates those who cruelly interdict the Christian people from it and furiously vociferate that no pestilence is more to be dreaded than that the reading of the Scriptures should be thrown open to the common people — for the apostle here addresses men and women of all ranks, and would not have them take a slight taste merely, but would have it dwell, have a settled abode, and richly, so that they aim to advance more every day. Take the word of Christ to mean the whole of Scripture, endited by the Spirit of Christ and testifying of him, or more especially the gospel, the word concerning his person and offices, peace and pardon by his blood, justification by his righteousness and salvation through his obedience and death. And conclude that life must be so regulated that whatever we say or do is wholly governed by the authority of Christ and has an eye to his glory as its mark, all our aims setting out with invocation of Christ and being subservient to his glory; from invocation follows the blessing of God, and thanks are to be given to the Father because through him we obtain every good thing.

Give the manuscript evidence for the peace of Christ — a long list of uncials, the Syriac, Arabic, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Vulgate and Old Latin, with several of the fathers, on which evidence Griesbach inserted it in the text. Then say: let the peace of Christ judge, decide and govern in your hearts as the judge does in the Olympic contests. No heart is right with God where that peace does not rule, and the continual prevalence of it is the decisive proof that the heart is right; when a man loses his peace it is an awful proof that he has lost something else, that he has given way to evil and grieved the Spirit of God — while peace rules, all is safe. Add that you cannot have peace with God nor among each other unless you continue in unity as one body depending on him who is your only head. Elsewhere, more briefly, read the verb as reward rather than umpire, so that the peace shall sway every temper, affection and thought as the reward of your preceding love and obedience. On the indwelling word, say the doctrine of Christ should be their constant study, frequently preached, explained and enforced; and see here an allusion to the Presence which dwelt in the tabernacle and first temple, with the rabbinic maxim that in whatever place the Law is, the Presence is with it — wherever God’s word is seriously read, heard or preached, there is God himself. Complain that through bad pointing the verse is not very intelligible, and insist that the members be distinguished so that in all wisdom goes forward with the teaching and admonishing, the original not merely bearing this but absolutely requiring it. Then attack the singing commonly used in congregations as a congeries of unmeaning sounds associated to bundles of nonsensical and often ridiculous repetitions, which both deprave and disgrace the Church; melody, the most proper for devotional music, is now sacrificed to an exuberant harmony requiring many kinds of voices and instruments to support it, by which preposterous means the simplicity of Christian worship is destroyed and edification prevented, and how few of those employed in it continue to sing with grace in their hearts. Elsewhere say that the word of Christ is the whole of Scripture, and that so calling it asserts the divinity of the Master; that it is to dwell, not make a short stay or an occasional visit, but take up its stated residence, and richly, in the largest measure, so as to fill and govern the whole soul. On the closing rule, begin with him and end with him, invoking his name in all you do; observe that doing everything in the name of God is as rational as it is pious, and then digress to the Mohammedans, who never undertake a work, eat meat or write a book without prefacing all with the name of the most merciful and compassionate God — not only books of devotion but books of arts and sciences, tales, romances and poetry, and even a production of the most abominable kind. Add that praises as well as prayers must ascend to God through the Mediator.

Having exhorted them to be thankful, show them the way. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly — the teaching, the doctrines, the exhortation in which He says that the present life is nothing, nor yet its good things; if we know this we shall yield to no hardships whatever. He said not simply let it be in you, but let it dwell in you, and richly, with great abundance. Hearken, as many as are worldly and have the charge of wife and children: to you especially he commits the reading of the Scriptures, and that not to be done lightly nor in any sort of way, but with much earnestness. For as the rich in money can bear fine and damages, so he that is rich in the doctrines of philosophy will bear not poverty only but all calamities easily, and more easily than that one — for the rich man, by discharging the fine, must needs be impoverished and found wanting, and if he should often suffer in that way will no longer be able to bear it; but in this case it is not so, for we do not expend our wholesome thoughts when it is necessary for us to bear what we would not choose, but they abide with us continually. And elsewhere, where the command to sing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs is quoted, cite it among the proofs that the Holy Ghost subsists and lives and speaks; and where the name of the Lord is in question, show from the passage where the Lord proclaimed the name of the Lord before Moses that the Son was with the Father.

debates: Whether the text reads the peace of God or the peace of Christ.
Whether the governing verb means to act as umpire or to award as reward.
Where the clause in all wisdom belongs, with the teaching before or the singing after.
Whether being thankful means gratitude for favours or sweetness of manners.
Whether the word of Christ means the whole of Scripture or the gospel in particular.
outliers: Four expositors independently prefer the peace of Christ, and one names the editor who put it in the text.
Wesley alone abandons the umpire of the games and reads the verb as reward.
Calvin turns the verse against those of his own day who forbade the people the Scriptures.
Chrysostom commits Scripture reading particularly to the married and worldly, and argues it from the economics of paying a fine.
Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson take three distinct positions on where one comma falls.
Barnes and Ellicott independently claim that hymns shape a church’s theology more than its preaching or its creeds.
Ellicott traces the emphasis on masters and servants in the following code to the presence of the runaway slave Onesimus.

18.pericope_label: Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as it is fit in the Lord — husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them — children, obey your parents in all things — fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged

schools.summary: For the most part refer the reader to the parallel passage and give only the verse numbers. Where you do comment: on the fitness in the Lord, send the reader to the grand description in the other epistle, this fitness resting on Christian unity. Note that the article distinguishes class from class and with the vocative is best rendered ye wives, that the word rendered own is genuine in the parallel but not here, and that the verb for subjection has a military air, common for such obedience, obedience in government being essential as the same word shows elsewhere. Call the construction an idiomatic use of the imperfect indicative with verbs of propriety in present time. Add that wives have rights and privileges, but that recognition of the husband’s leadership is essential to a well-ordered home — only the assumption is that the husband has a head, and a wise one. On the husbands, read the imperatives as habits: keep on loving, and stop being bitter or do not have the habit of being bitter; call this the sin of husbands, note that the verb occurs in the New Testament only here and in one other book, and say that the bitter word rankles in the soul; add that the word is used metaphorically only in this passage and literally elsewhere, and that the sense is properly grow not bitter, suffer not yourselves to be exasperated. On the children, take the verb as listening under, as one looking up, and note that the hard part is not occasional obedience but continual — surely a Christian parent will make no unreasonable demand, but nowhere does modern civilisation show more weakness than here, and waves of lawlessness sweep over the world because the child was not taught to obey. On the last verse, say that the reading followed by our version, provoke not to anger, is borrowed from the parallel epistle, and that the true reading is provoke not to emulation, so that what is forbidden is a constant and restless stimulation, the spurring of the willing horse, which will end in failure and despondency; or else keep the ordinary sense and note that the verb occurs twice only in the New Testament, in a good sense elsewhere where it means to stimulate, and here in a bad sense meaning to nag, and that as a habit. On the discouragement, distinguish flattery from encouragement: children should not be so praised as to make them vain, but they should be commended when they do well, and the desire of praise should not be the principle from which they act, though they should feel that a parent’s approbation is desirable. He who always finds fault, who is never satisfied, who scolds and frets let the child do as he will, breaks his spirit and destroys in the delicate texture of his soul all desire of doing well; the child in despair soon gives over every effort to please and becomes sullen, morose, stupid and indifferent, since all he does meets the same reception. And add that one does not have to know much of the sorrows of childhood, as witnessed by runaway children and even child suicides.

Observe first that the apostle proceeds from the duties that belong to them as church members to those that concern them in their own houses and families — husbands and wives, parents and children, masters and servants — showing that the gospel does not break in upon but establishes the duties of common and civil life; then refer the reader to your own notes elsewhere. Where you do expound, say that these are the particular duties, so called, which depend on the calling of individuals, and that since almost everything necessary has been said in the commentary on the other epistle it were superfluous to take up many words; add only what suits this passage. The command to wives is clear, but what follows is of doubtful signification, for some connect it thus, be subject in the Lord, as it is fit; view it rather as it is fit in the Lord, that is, according to the appointment of the Lord, so that he confirms the subjection of wives by the authority of God. Require love and gentleness on the part of husbands, because there is danger lest they should abuse their authority in the way of tyranny. On the children, ask what is to be done if parents should be disposed to constrain them to anything unlawful — will they too obey without reservation? It were worse than unreasonable that the authority of men should prevail at the expense of neglecting God; understand therefore as implied what is expressed in the parallel epistle. But then ask to what purpose the term of universality is employed, and answer that it is to show that obedience must be rendered not merely to just commands but also to such as are unreasonable, grievous and rigorous, since many make themselves compliant only where the command is not inconvenient. Let children consider this one thing, that whoever their parents may be, they have been allotted to them by the providence of God, who by his appointment makes children subject to their parents: that they may refuse nothing however difficult or disagreeable; that in things indifferent they may give deference to the station their parents occupy; and that they may not put themselves on a footing of equality with their parents in the way of questioning, debating or disputing — it being always understood that conscience is not to be infringed upon. Then prohibit parents from exercising an immoderate harshness, lest their children be so disheartened as to be incapable of receiving any honourable training, for we see from daily experience the advantage of a liberal education.

Note that the epistles most taken up in displaying the glory of divine grace are the most particular in pressing the duties of the several relations, and that we must never separate the privileges and duties of gospel religion. On submission, observe that the word is the same used of our duty to magistrates, and give the reason from the order of things: Adam was first formed, then Eve; Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression; he was first in the creation and last in the transgression. It is agreeable to the order of nature and the reason of things as well as to the appointment of God. But then it is submission not to a rigorous lord or absolute tyrant who may do his will and is without restraint, but to a husband, and to her own husband, who stands in the nearest relation and is under strict engagements to proper duty too; and it is fit in the Lord, becoming the relation, an instance of obedience to the authority of Christ. On the other side, husbands must love with tender and faithful affection, as Christ loved the church and as their own bodies, and must not use them unkindly with harsh language or severe treatment, for the woman was made for the man, yet neither is the man without the woman. On children, say they must be willing to do all their lawful commands and be at their direction, as those who have a natural right and are fitter to direct them than themselves; add that the parallel epistle requires them to honour as well as obey, since the obedience of the life must proceed from the esteem of the mind, and that this is the first commandment with promise, dutiful children being the most likely to prosper and enjoy long life. And on parents: let not your authority be exercised with rigour and severity but with kindness and gentleness, lest you raise their passions and discourage them in their duty, and by holding the reins too tight make them fly out with greater fierceness — the bad temper and example of imprudent parents often proving a stumbling-block in their children’s way. It is by the tenderness of parents and the dutifulness of children that God ordinarily furnishes his church with a seed to serve him.

Say that the apostle, having done with general directions, comes to the particular duties commonly called relative, because they belong only to persons in certain situations and are not incumbent on all — no woman has the duty of a wife to perform but she who is one — and that the directions to wives, husbands, children, parents, servants and masters are so exactly the same in substance as those in the parallel epistle that there is no need to repeat what was said there. On the fitness, say simply that God commands it and it is both proper and decent; and elsewhere, that the verb is properly a military term, alluding to the entire submission that soldiers pay to their general. On the husbands, say that wherever bitterness is, there love is wanting, and where love is wanting in the married life there is hell upon earth; and add that bitterness may be present without any appearance of anger, either in word or spirit. On the children, take the qualification strictly: obey in everything your parents command which is not contrary to the will or word of God. On the last verse refer again to the parallel, and say only that discouragement may occasion their turning either desperate or stupid.

Ask first why he does not give these commands everywhere and in all the epistles, but only here and in three others; answer that probably there were dissensions in these cities, or probably they were correct in other respects so that it was expedient they should hear of these things — though what he says to these he says to all. Note the great resemblance this epistle bears to the other in these matters, either because it was not fitting to write of them to men now at peace who still needed instruction in high doctrines, or because for persons comforted under trials it were superfluous to hear on these subjects; and conjecture that in this place the church was now well grounded, and that these things are said as in finishing. Then on the command itself: be subject for God’s sake, because this adorneth you, not them; for the subjection meant is not that which is due to a master, nor yet that alone which is of nature, but that which is for God’s sake. And on the children, say that while honouring our heavenly Father we must honour also the fathers of our flesh, since the Lord himself so appointed in the Law and the Prophets; let the commandment be especially observed by those present who have fathers and mothers. For the Lord said not, he that loveth father or mother is not worthy of me, lest thou shouldest from ignorance mistake what was rightly written, but he added, more than me. When our fathers on earth are of a contrary mind to our Father in heaven, then we must obey Christ’s word; but when they put no obstacle to godliness in our way, and we are carried away by ingratitude and forgetting their benefits hold them in contempt, then the oracle will have place which says that he who curseth father or mother shall die the death.

debates: Whether in the Lord governs the fitness or the subjection.
Whether the fault forbidden to fathers is exasperation or restless stimulation.
How far the word all extends when parents command what is unlawful.
Whether the command to wives borrows a military sense.
Why the household rules are given in this letter and not in most others.
outliers: Chrysostom infers the state of the church from the fact that the rules are given at all.
Three of the fullest expositors withhold comment here and refer the reader to the parallel epistle.
Calvin uses the word all to argue that unreasonable commands are also to be obeyed, not to widen the exception.
Cyril of Jerusalem locates the exception in a saying of Christ that turns on one added word.
Ellicott rejects the received reading and makes over-encouragement, not exasperation, the thing forbidden.
Robertson and Wesley independently hear a military term in the verb for submission.
Robertson qualifies the command to wives by the condition that the husband have a wise head.

22.pericope_label: Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh — and whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men — knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance — but he that doeth wrong shall receive for the wrong which he hath done, and there is no respect of persons

schools.summary: Fix the extent of the obedience first: in all things relating to the body and bodily service, not to the conscience and religious worship; in things worldly and not spiritual; in all things within a master’s power and lawful for him to command; in all things fitting and proper for a servant to do; and even in such things as may be difficult, troublesome and disagreeable to the flesh. Then raise the question of scope: some have thought that the verses following regard the Colossians in general and the performance of any and all good works by them, but by their connection with the preceding verse and with the beginning of the next chapter they concern servants only, and what they do under that character in the discharge of their duty. On the reward, encourage Christian servants who may receive little or nothing from their earthly and carnal masters, since they shall be treated as children by the Lord and possessed of an eternal inheritance after their labour is over; call the heavenly glory a reward because you are speaking to servants and use language agreeable to them, and say that though they may have no reward in this world, there is verily one for them in the world to come. But guard it: though it is not given for working, it is given to those that do good and continue in well doing, whose works follow them and do not go before them; it is enjoyed after their work is over, as the servant receives his wages at evening when his work is done; and it is received not as a reward of debt but of grace. Say also that anything else here requires no exposition, having been expounded already on the parallel epistle, except two expressions. By the first the apostle means that service is done to men in such a way that Christ at the same time holds supremacy of dominion and is the supreme master, which is choice consolation for all who are under subjection, since while they willingly serve their masters their services are acceptable to Christ as though rendered to him; and from this gather that the very thing bestowed in reward of works is freely given us by God, for the inheritance comes of adoption. By the second, comfort them again: if they are oppressed by the unjust cruelty of their masters, God himself will take vengeance and will not overlook the injuries inflicted on them on the ground that they are slaves, since there is no respect of persons — for this consideration might diminish their courage, if they imagined that God had no regard for them and that their miseries gave him no concern. And since it often happens that servants themselves endeavour to avenge injurious and cruel treatment, obviate that evil by admonishing them to wait patiently for the judgment of God. On the wrongdoer, allow it of both sides: of servants who wrong their masters through sloth and idleness, neglecting their business, embezzling their goods and defrauding them of their substance; and of masters who wrong their servants by withholding proper food and raiment, by cheating them of their wages, giving none at all or too little or detaining them too long, and by hard language and harder blows.

Note that the word is really lords, and that these Christian slaves had Christ as lord, but even so were to obey their lords in the flesh. Point out that the compound rendered eye-service is another word of the apostle’s own, occurring here and in the parallel only and elsewhere only in Christian writers after him, an easy and expressive compound for service while the master’s eye was on the slave and no longer; that men-pleasers is a late compound found only in the Greek Old Testament and in this writer; that singleness of heart is an old and expressive word from a root meaning simple, without folds; and that the fear enjoined is of the Lord rather than of the lords according to the flesh. On working heartily, say it is from the soul and not with mere eye-service, that the parallel adds with good will in explanation of the phrase, and that doing it as to the Lord even when it is done to men is the highest test of worth-while service — if it were only always true. On the reward, take the verb as an old one meaning to get back or recover, and the noun as the full recompense, given back in return, a word of the Greek Old Testament occurring only here in the New; and suggest that the closing words may be better read as an imperative, keep on serving, as his slaves and gladly so. On the last verse, say it is not clear whether the wrongdoer is the master or the slave, that it is true of either, and that one commentator interprets it of both, shall receive back the wrong which he did — this being a general law of life and of God, and fair and square. Elsewhere say the wrongdoer is clearly the master, citing the parallel, though of course the phrase cannot be limited to him. On the closing clause note that there is respect of persons with men but not with God, and that the word is patterned after the Hebrew. Add, as an aside on the text, that the first verse of the following chapter belongs to this one.

Refer the reader to the parallel epistle for the substance, and gloss only the hard words. Eye-service is being more diligent under their eye than at other times; singleness of heart is a simple intention of doing right without looking any farther; and fearing God means acting from that principle. On working heartily, take it as cheerfully and diligently, and draw the contrast: men-pleasers are soon dejected and made angry, while the single-hearted are never displeased or disappointed, because they have another aim, which the good or evil treatment of those they serve cannot disappoint. On the reward, speak directly to men who own nothing — here you have neither lands nor property, you are servants or slaves, be not discouraged, you have an inheritance in store; be faithful to God and to your employers, and Christ will give you a heavenly inheritance. On the wrongdoer, take him to be the unfaithful servant: it is possible for such a one to wrong and defraud his master in a great variety of ways without being detected, but let him remember that God sees him and will punish him for his breach of honesty and trust; wasting, or not taking proper care of, the goods of a master is such a wrong as God will resent, and he that is unfaithful in what is little will be unfaithful in much if he have opportunity, God alone being the defence against an unfaithful servant. And on the closing clause, say that God neither esteems nor despises any man because of his outward condition and circumstances, for every man is in the eye of God what he is in his soul: if holy, loved; if wicked, despised and rejected.

debates: Whether the verses on working heartily address servants only or the whole church.
How an inheritance received as a reward can still be of grace.
Whether the wrongdoer of the last verse is the master or the servant.
How far the obedience owed in all things extends.
Whether the closing clause about service is indicative or imperative.
outliers: Gill and Calvin independently reconcile the reward with grace, by different routes.
Ellicott, Robertson and Calvin take three different views of who does the wrong.
Robertson reports an earlier commentator applying the last verse to master and servant at once.
Calvin gives a pastoral reason for insisting that God will avenge: servants otherwise avenge themselves.
Wesley turns single-heartedness into a defence against disappointment rather than a duty.
Robertson notes two of the compounds in the passage are coinages found only in this writer.
Robertson remarks that the opening verse of the next chapter belongs to this one.
